title: Present perfect simple and continuous
tagline: Started in the past, still true now — the tense that links yesterday to today.
exam: Speaking Part 1 — talking about your experiences
why: B1 Preliminary loves asking about your life so far — jobs, places, things you have or haven't done — and that means have/has + past participle, not the past simple. The cloze and the open cloze both test for vs since, been vs gone and the exact moment when already becomes yesterday, so this is one of the highest-value grammar points in the whole exam.

hook.text: Sofia: “How long have you worked at the bakery?” Liam: “I've worked there since June — I've just finished my first month!” Nadia: “Have you ever made bread yourself?”
hook.ask: Liam started the job in the past, but he's still doing it now. Find the verb forms that connect his past start to the present — what pattern do they follow?

watch_out.why: Since connects a past start to now, so it needs the present perfect, not the present simple.

watch_out.wrong: I have worked here since three months.
watch_out.right: I've worked here for three months / since June.
watch_out.why: For + a length of time, since + a point in time — don't mix them up.
Yesterday is a finished time word, so it needs the past simple, never the present perfect.

watch_out.wrong: She has went to the market.
watch_out.why: The past participle of go is gone, not went.

watch_out.wrong: She has been to the shop, she isn't back yet.
watch_out.right: She's gone to the shop — she isn't back yet.
watch_out.why: Been to = went and came back; gone to = went and is still there.

watch_out.wrong: How long do you work here?
watch_out.why: A question about an action that started in the past and continues needs the present perfect.

l1.why: Spanish uses the present tense with desde; English needs the present perfect for an action that continues to now.

l1.wrong: I have finished the homework already, yesterday.
l1.why: Already goes with the present perfect (no exact time); a specific time word like yesterday needs the past simple instead.
An experience up to now (nunca + present perfect in Spanish) needs the present perfect in English too.

l1.es: Fue a la tienda (y ya volvió).
l1.wrong: She has gone to the shop and she's back.
l1.right: She's been to the shop and she's back.
l1.why: Been to shows a completed round trip; gone to means the person is still away.

remember.trick: Started in the past, still true? Use HAVE!
remember.tip: If you can add since or for and the action is still true now, use the present perfect, not the past simple.

can_do: I can talk about experiences and unfinished time with for, since, ever and never.
I can use just, already, yet and still with the present perfect.
I can choose between the present perfect and the past simple, and between been and gone.
summary: Present perfect = have/has + past participle, connecting the past to now.
For + a length of time, since + a starting point, ever/never for experience, just/already/yet/still for recent news.
A specific past time word (yesterday, last year) always needs the past simple, not the present perfect.
Been to = went and came back; gone to = went and hasn't come back yet.
Present perfect continuous (have/has been + -ing) focuses on the activity itself, often with how long.
